nodes.title: Non-Relational (NoSQL) Data: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Non-relational (NoSQL) data stores trade the rigid table schema of relational databases for flexible models that scale horizontally for large or rapidly changing data. DP-900 (Azure Data Fundamentals) tests the four NoSQL model types and how Azure Cosmos DB delivers them.

flashcards.front: What are the four common non-relational data models?
flashcards.back: Key-value (a key maps to an opaque value), document (self-describing JSON/BSON documents), column-family (rows with dynamic column sets grouped into families), and graph (nodes and edges modeling relationships).

flashcards.front: What does 'schema-on-read' mean for NoSQL stores?
flashcards.back: Data is stored without enforcing a fixed schema on write; structure is interpreted by the application when the data is read. This allows items in the same container to have different fields and lets the schema evolve freely.

flashcards.front: When does NoSQL beat relational storage?
flashcards.back: When you need massive horizontal scale, high write/read throughput with flexible or evolving schemas, and can favor performance and availability over complex multi-table joins and strict ACID transactions — e.g., IoT telemetry, catalogs, user profiles.

flashcards.front: Why is choosing a good partition key important in Azure Cosmos DB?
flashcards.back: Cosmos DB distributes data across logical partitions by partition key; a well-chosen key spreads requests and storage evenly to avoid 'hot' partitions, enabling elastic horizontal scale and consistent performance.

questions.q: A workload requires globally distributed, low-latency reads and writes for a flexible JSON document store. Which Azure Cosmos DB API is the natural fit?
choices: The API for NoSQL (formerly Core SQL), which natively stores JSON documents at scale

The API for PostgreSQL, which exposes a relational interface over distributed tables using JSON functions for document queries — the PostgreSQL API provides SQL semantics over Cosmos DB; JSON documents are natively stored and indexed by the NoSQL Core SQL API, not the relational PostgreSQL API
The API for Apache Cassandra, which is designed for wide-column key-value workloads
The API for Apache Gremlin, which is purpose-built for property-graph traversal use
questions.explanation: Cosmos DB's API for NoSQL (the renamed Core/SQL API) is the document model, storing JSON natively and queryable with a SQL-like syntax. PostgreSQL is relational, Cassandra is wide-column, and Gremlin is graph-traversal — all valid Cosmos DB APIs but mismatched to a JSON document workload.

questions.q: You need to store millions of unstructured log files of varying sizes for cheap, durable archival. Which Azure storage service is most appropriate?
choices: Azure Blob Storage with the cool or archive access tier set on each individual blob
Azure Files, which exposes the data as an SMB or NFS share mounted on virtual machines
Azure Table Storage, which holds semi-structured key-attribute rows for fast lookups
Azure SQL Database, which keeps the records in normalized tables with strong indexes
questions.explanation: Azure Blob Storage is built for massive volumes of unstructured object data and offers Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive access tiers to optimize cost for rarely accessed content. Azure Files targets shared file-system access; Table Storage stores structured key-attribute records; Azure SQL is a relational engine — none are designed for cheap blob archival.

questions.q: A retailer needs a globally distributed database with single-digit-millisecond latency and the ability to tune how strictly reads reflect the latest writes, ranging from strong to eventual. Which Azure service offers configurable consistency levels designed for this?
choices: Azure SQL Database with read replicas placed in two additional regions
Azure Cosmos DB, which offers five well-defined configurable consistency levels
Azure Cache for Redis configured in a geo-replicated active cluster
Azure Blob Storage with read-access geo-redundant storage enabled
questions.explanation: Azure Cosmos DB is the globally distributed database that exposes five well-defined consistency levels (strong, bounded staleness, session, consistent prefix, eventual) with low-latency reads and writes worldwide. Azure SQL Database read replicas provide read scale-out but not the five-level consistency spectrum Cosmos DB defines. Azure Cache for Redis is an in-memory cache, not a primary globally distributed database with tunable consistency. Blob Storage with RA-GRS replicates objects but offers no configurable database consistency levels.

questions.q: A data platform stores hierarchical files in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 and needs efficient directory-level operations such as renaming and securing entire folders. Which Azure Storage capability provides the true folder hierarchy that makes these operations efficient?
choices: Lifecycle management policies that move blobs between access tiers on a schedule
The hierarchical namespace, which organizes objects into a true directory structure
Soft delete, which retains deleted blobs for a configurable retention period
Object replication, which asynchronously copies blobs between two storage accounts
questions.explanation: The hierarchical namespace is the feature that turns a storage account into Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, giving a true directory structure so folder-level operations such as rename and access control are atomic and efficient. Lifecycle management only moves blobs between tiers and does not provide directory semantics. Soft delete retains deleted data but creates no folder hierarchy. Object replication copies blobs across accounts and is unrelated to directory-level operations.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A data engineer is sorting incoming sources into the three classic categories. The first source is a CSV of customer orders with a strict header row and the same column types in every row. The second is a directory of JSON logs whose schema varies. The third is a dump of opaque PDF files. Which description fits the first source — the classic 'structured' category — for the DP-900 exam?
choices: Data that conforms to a rigid, predefined schema with named columns and consistent types per row — typically stored in relational tables and queried with SQL
Data whose schema is implied by the file format and varies across records — typically stored as JSON, XML, or Parquet on object storage and queried with a schema-on-read engine
Opaque binary content with no machine-readable schema — typically images, audio, video, and PDF documents, stored on blob storage and indexed via metadata
Tabular content extracted via OCR from scanned forms — the only category whose ingestion pipeline requires a manual human review step before processing
questions.explanation: Structured data fits a predefined schema with strongly typed columns, classically stored in relational tables. Unstructured data (images, audio, video) has no schema. Semi-structured data (JSON, Avro) has a flexible schema that can vary record to record. Storage location is unrelated to the structured/unstructured classification.

questions.q: A team is choosing between two workload categories for a new payments service. Option A executes thousands of short, concurrent reads and writes per second against a normalised schema with strict consistency. Option B aggregates billions of historical rows and returns multi-dimensional summaries to a BI tool. Which workload pattern fits option A — OLTP — best?
choices: Long-running analytical aggregations against billions of rows, returning multi-dimensional results — OLAP workloads scan large datasets and take minutes or hours per query; they do not match the low-latency, high-concurrency, per-second throughput profile of OLTP systems described here
Many small concurrent transactions with low latency, strict consistency, and ACID guarantees against a normalised schema — measured in transactions per second

Sequential batch processing of nightly files where each job runs for hours — batch jobs are not concurrent, do not require strict ACID guarantees per transaction, do not use a normalised schema for online writes, and prioritise throughput over per-transaction latency

Read-mostly archival lookups against immutable historical partitions — archival stores prioritise storage efficiency over write consistency; writes are appended once at month-end and never modified, so per-transaction consistency guarantees are irrelevant
questions.explanation: Online Transaction Processing (OLTP) systems are optimized for high volumes of small, concurrent, low-latency read/write transactions — for example, e-commerce orders or banking transfers. Large analytical scans, training workloads, and nightly ETL aggregations are characteristic of OLAP and data-warehouse systems, not OLTP.

questions.q: A directory of customer records arrives as JSON files where some records include an optional 'middleName' field and others omit it entirely. The data conforms to a flexible, self-describing format rather than a rigid table. Which data category does this represent for the DP-900 exam?
choices: Structured data, because every record is stored as text in a file
Semi-structured data, because the format is self-describing and the schema can vary between records
Unstructured data, because JSON files have no machine-readable schema at all
Relational data, because the records describe customers that map to a customer table
questions.explanation: JSON whose fields vary record to record is semi-structured: it carries a self-describing, flexible schema rather than a rigid one. It is not structured data, which requires a fixed, predefined schema with consistent typed columns. It is not unstructured — JSON is machine-readable and tags each value, unlike images or video. It is not inherently relational; describing customers does not make the storage format a relational table.

questions.q: In Power BI, which artifact is published by report authors and reused by many reports as the single source of truth for measures and relationships?
choices: A dashboard, which pins tiles from multiple reports onto a single landing page — a dashboard assembles visual tiles from published reports; it does not define tables, relationships, measures, or DAX calculations that reports consume
A workspace, which is a container that holds reports, datasets, dataflows, and apps
A semantic model (dataset), which defines tables, relationships, measures, and DAX
A report, which is the visual canvas with pages of charts, slicers, and visuals
questions.explanation: A Power BI semantic model — historically called a dataset — defines the tables, relationships, calculated columns, and DAX measures that visuals consume. Multiple reports can connect to one shared semantic model. Dashboards are pinned-tile summaries, workspaces are containers, and reports are the visual layer built on top of a semantic model.

questions.q: An organization wants a single managed analytics store that holds large volumes of historical sales data optimized for read-heavy aggregations across many dimensions, feeding a BI tool. Which type of data store is the best fit?
choices: A data warehouse, optimized for analytical queries and large-scale aggregation over historical data
An OLTP database, optimized for many small concurrent transactions with strict consistency
A message queue, optimized for buffering events between producers and consumers
A key-value cache, optimized for sub-millisecond lookups of individual items by key
questions.explanation: A data warehouse is purpose-built for analytical, read-heavy aggregation over large historical datasets feeding BI tools, matching the requirement. An OLTP database targets high volumes of small concurrent transactions, not multi-dimensional analytical scans. A message queue buffers events for transport and does not store data for analytical querying. A key-value cache accelerates single-item lookups by key, not large aggregations across dimensions.

questions.q: In a Power BI workflow, an analyst connects to several sources, removes columns, changes data types, and merges queries before the data is loaded into the model. Which Power BI component performs these data preparation and transformation steps?
choices: Power Query, the data preparation engine where sources are shaped and transformed before loading
A report, the visual canvas where charts and slicers present the loaded data
A dashboard, the page of pinned tiles summarizing content from one or more reports
DAX, the formula language used to define calculated measures over the loaded model
questions.explanation: Power Query is Power BI's data preparation engine where you connect to sources and apply transformation steps such as removing columns, changing types, and merging queries before the data loads into the model. A report is the visual layer that presents already-loaded data. A dashboard assembles pinned tiles and performs no transformation. DAX defines measures and calculations over the loaded model rather than preparing or shaping incoming source data.

questions.q: You need a fully managed relational service that supports almost the full SQL Server feature set, including SQL Agent and cross-database queries. Which Azure offering should you choose?
choices: Azure SQL Database (single database), which exposes a subset of SQL Server features
Azure SQL Managed Instance, which offers near-100% SQL Server compatibility as PaaS
SQL Server on an Azure Virtual Machine, which is an IaaS deployment you must patch
Azure Database for PostgreSQL, which is open-source PostgreSQL hosted as a service
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Managed Instance is the PaaS option engineered for near-100% compatibility with on-premises SQL Server, including SQL Agent, cross-database queries, CLR, and Service Broker. Azure SQL Database (single/elastic) trades some features for simplicity. SQL Server on an Azure VM is IaaS — fully compatible but unmanaged. PostgreSQL is a different engine.

questions.q: A startup wants to host an existing PostgreSQL application in Azure as a fully managed service so they do not patch the OS or the database engine, while keeping standard PostgreSQL compatibility. Which Azure service should they choose?
choices: PostgreSQL installed on an Azure Virtual Machine that the team patches and backs up themselves
Azure Database for PostgreSQL, a fully managed PaaS offering of the PostgreSQL engine
Azure SQL Database, a fully managed service running the Microsoft SQL Server engine
Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL emulated through the API for NoSQL document model
questions.explanation: Azure Database for PostgreSQL is a managed PaaS that runs the standard PostgreSQL engine, so the team gets compatibility without patching the OS or engine. PostgreSQL on an Azure VM is IaaS and requires the team to patch and manage the OS and database. Azure SQL Database runs the SQL Server engine, not PostgreSQL. The API for NoSQL is a document model and does not emulate PostgreSQL relational compatibility.
